headline: High: shared filesystem/git and broad egress make Claude Code dangerous with a write-capable pair, while the content-writing peer adds little isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is a content-writing agent with broad network egress; profile B reads/writes repo files and uses MCP, so A’s generated content can be fed into B through files or terminal output. The pair lacks any provenance or isolation mechanism in either profile, so prompt-like instructions embedded in A’s outputs could steer B. This is interaction-based, not provably blocked.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs instructions inside text that agent_b later ingests from files or stdin/stdout
IF agent_b treats file content or MCP payloads as trusted instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Strip instructions from A’s outputs before handing them to B
Use a fixed handoff template between agents
Disable MCP for the handoff session
Require B to summarize and verify A’s output before acting
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: B explicitly reads and writes filesystem content and handles git history, while A has broad network egress. If A is given sensitive files or repo content and then forwards or summarizes them, B can transmit that material off-host. The profiles show no isolation or DLP controls, so leakage is plausible in default use even though the exact data class is not specified.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared working directory
IF agent_a is prompted to summarize or relay content that agent_b read from disk
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared cwd
Run B in a scrubbed repo clone
Block outbound network for A during sensitive tasks
Review git diffs before any push
requires-engineering: add content filtering or DLP

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B has write_filesystem and modify_git_state with shared state via filesystem and git only; A is a content-writing agent that can also influence the same workspace through outputs. The pair therefore has overlapping mutable access to the same artifacts, and the profile gives no locking or coordination primitive. That makes concurrent edits and git-state corruption a default danger.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or cwd
IF agent_a’s generated edits are applied while agent_b is modifying git state
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize edits through one agent at a time
Use git worktrees per agent
Check for clean tree before commits
requires-engineering: add file-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate prose or code-like content, and B can act on repo files and shell commands. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into commits or shell actions. The profiles do not show a verification gate, but they also do not prove fully autonomous downstream actions, so medium is the higher justified severity.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a’s output as direct input to shell commands or commits
IF no human or automated verification step checks A’s claims before B acts
mitigations: Require B to cite source files before acting
Insert a human review step for commits
Use dry-run mode for shell actions
Ask B to restate assumptions before execution
requires-engineering: add verification checksums

E_compliance.rationale: The only concrete compliance-relevant fact is B’s handling of git credentials and Anthropic API key material; A’s profile does not show regulated data classes or residency constraints. No PHI/EU PII mismatch is evidenced, so the pairwise compliance risk is limited to ordinary secret-handling hygiene rather than a documented breach pathway.
conditions: IF secrets are stored in files that both agents can read
IF regulated data is introduced into the shared workspace
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared repo
Rotate exposed credentials after testing
Use environment variables instead of files
Restrict access to the terminal session
requires-engineering: separate secret-bearing workflows
